progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: B6c: a polypeptide is a chain of amino acids in the order set by the codons and must fold before it works; codon chart use with mRNA codons. B6b: a gene is the stretch of DNA that codes for a polypeptide; a changed template base changes a codon. B4: a surviving copying error is a mutation. B1: alleles are versions of a gene and a clone has the same genes as its parent. Year 11 Biology: enzymes and active sites, cells and membranes, haemoglobin carries oxygen in red blood cells. Not assumed: protein jobs as a classification, why chains fold, levels of structure, phenotype, genotype, polygenic, gene-environment interaction.
progression.startsWith: One hydrangea cloned into two gardens that flower blue and pink, with the question of how a chain of amino acids becomes a trait you can see and how identical genes give different results.
progression.stopsAfter: Naming five jobs proteins do with an example of each; explaining why a chain folds into one shape and the four levels of structure; explaining why shape decides function and why a changed amino acid can, but need not, change it; tracing sickle cell from one base change to the trait; saying why genes become traits skips steps; defining genotype and phenotype; explaining a same-genotype, different-phenotype case with its mechanism; assessing genes and environment together; analysing why polypeptide synthesis matters; applying all of it to a temperature-sensitive enzyme and to two base changes read from a codon chart. No alpha helix and beta sheet by name, no gene regulation, no mutation types, no epigenetics.
progression.nextLesson: B8: sources of genetic variation, where the different genotypes in one family come from.

teaching.task: Explain how a chain of amino acids becomes a trait, and why the same genes can give different results in different environments.
teaching.causalExplanation: The twenty amino acids differ: some avoid water and tuck into the middle of the chain, some carry opposite charges that attract, and two cysteines can lock together, so the order of amino acids decides which parts meet and therefore the shape. Proteins work by fitting, so a change in an active site can stop the fit, while a change far from it or to the same amino acid may not. In sickle cell, one base change turns a glutamate codon into a valine codon, and valine avoids water, so with two copies and low oxygen the haemoglobin molecules stick into fibres that bend the red cells, which block small vessels and break down early. Genes do not become traits directly: the gene codes for a polypeptide, which folds into a protein, which changes what a cell does. The same genotype can give different phenotypes because the environment changes what the proteins produce, for example soil aluminium binding the hydrangea pigment, without changing the alleles.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Opens on cloned hydrangeas of two colours and last video's chain, shows five protein jobs on real objects, builds the fold from the amino acids' differences, shows shape deciding the job, runs sickle cell as one full chain on a five-station strip, names genotype and phenotype after the causes, gives the hydrangea mechanism and height, weighs genes against environment, explains why synthesis matters, adds the memory aids, then asks two harder unseen items with a short pause and brief model answers.
teaching.openingDecision: The same genes give blue flowers in one garden and pink in another. How does a chain of amino acids become a trait you can see, and how can the same genes give different results?
teaching.understandingCheck: A Himalayan rabbit has dark fur only on its cool extremities, and a shaved back patch under an ice pack regrew dark: explain why and predict the fur of its young. Then in two snapdragon lines, read a codon chart to explain why a histidine to proline change in an active site gives white flowers while GAA to GAG leaves them red.
teaching.curriculumScope: Model the process of polypeptide synthesis and analyse its importance, assess how genes and environment affect phenotypic expression, and investigate the structure and function of proteins in living things (Module 5, ACSBL079 to ACSBL081). The video gives the knowledge an investigation needs and does not claim the practical. Gene regulation, mutation types, protein structure by name, carrier advantage and epigenetics are deferred.

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer, painted hydrangea, enzyme and substrate, red blood cell, normal and sickle cell, muscle cell, blood typing, snapdragon and rabbit plates, and coded bead chains that fold, a chain-to-trait strip of five stations, haemoglobin fibres, a range bar and a trait spectrum. B6c beads carry a printed three-letter name, never colour only. Blue and green are used only inside the painted hydrangea plates.
design.transitionPlan: The painted hydrangea opens the lesson and the bead chain drifts in from the previous video; the jobs board builds tile by tile; the fold chain returns beside the enzyme plate; the chain-to-trait strip builds in the sickle cell scene and stays as a thin header to the synthesis scene; each attempt card clears the aids and its feedback shrinks the card to a strip and builds the model answer one point at a time; the next chip slides in; scene crossfade with settle.
